title: How Much Computation Does Every Forecast Need?Structured Block Skipping in Two Time-Series Foundation Models

paper.title: How Much Computation Does Every Forecast Need? Structured Block Skipping in Two Time-Series Foundation Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Time-series foundation models use the same network depth for every input, although forecasting windows differ in structure and difficulty. We test whether whole Transformer blocks can be removed at inference time in two pretrained models: Chronos-Bolt and TimesFM 2.5. Our bypasses avoid the original block computation and preserve the dense model exactly when all blocks are enabled. Masks are selected only on calibration windows and evaluated on 1,088 held-out windows from ETTh1, Traffic, Weather, and Exchange. At moderate sparsity, Chronos-Bolt with 7/11 candidate blocks and TimesFM with 16/20 blocks show little change in mean relative forecasting quality across datasets while reducing median A100 batch-1 latency by 11.2% and 13.4%. More aggressive TimesFM skipping accelerates inference further but substantially harms Traffic and Weather. Across both models, different equal-budget masks win on different windows, and a retrospective oracle significantly improves over the best static mask on every dataset. However, dataset-specific masks transfer inconsistently, and Chronos representations do not support reliable unseen-domain routing. These results establish cross-architecture structured redundancy and input-dependent opportunity, but not a deployable dynamic inference method.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Pretrained time-series foundation models (TSFMs) have recently emerged as general-purpose models for zero- and few-shot forecasting across heterogeneous domains ( Ansari et al., 2024 ; Das et al., 2024 ; Rasul et al., 2024 ; Woo et al., 2024 ; Goswami et al., 2024 ; Ekambaram et al., 2024 ) . Yet these models typically execute a fixed network for every input. This is undesirable when latency is constrained and potentially unnecessary when forecasting windows vary in predictability. Global compression reduces a network for all inputs. We ask a different question: does every input require the same structured subset of a pretrained TSFM? We study executable whole-block skipping without fine-tuning. Our goal is not to propose a router, but to establish whether there is useful opportunity for one. We measure static quality-compute curves using calibration-selected masks and real GPU latency, compare equal-cardinality masks across datasets, and compute a retrospective per-window oracle. Using Chronos-Bolt, we then test whether temporal features or frozen representations can predict useful masks across domains. We find: (1) removable computation is not model-specific: both Chronos-Bolt and the architecturally different decoder-only TimesFM admit moderate block skipping with real acceleration and limited aggregate quality change; (2) mask identity matters, especially in TimesFM, where the selected mask beats every one of 20 random masks at each sparse budget and dataset; and (3) both models have a significant per-window oracle advantage, but neither dataset identity nor tested Chronos features yield robust transferable routing. Static redundancy and input-dependent preference recur across models, while safe sparsity and routability remain architecture- and domain-dependent.

sections.heading: Time-series foundation models.
sections.text: Recent TSFMs pretrain on collections of heterogeneous time series to support transfer across datasets and domains. Chronos casts forecasting as token prediction ( Ansari et al., 2024 ) , TimesFM uses a decoder-only patched architecture ( Das et al., 2024 ) , and Lag-Llama targets probabilistic zero-shot forecasting ( Rasul et al., 2024 ) . Moirai and MOMENT broaden pretraining across datasets and tasks ( Woo et al., 2024 ; Goswami et al., 2024 ) , while Tiny Time Mixers emphasize compact models and efficient transfer ( Ekambaram et al., 2024 ) . Our question is complementary: rather than train a smaller model, we ask how much of an already pretrained TSFM must execute for each forecast.

sections.heading: Structured and input-dependent computation.
sections.text: Reducing depth at inference has a substantial history outside time-series forecasting. LayerDrop trains Transformers so subnetworks of different depths can be extracted at inference ( Fan et al., 2020 ) , while DynaBERT learns width- and depth-adaptive subnetworks through training and distillation ( Hou et al., 2020 ) . Input-dependent methods instead vary computation by example: adaptive computation time allocates a variable number of recurrent steps ( Graves, 2016 ) , SkipNet learns to bypass residual blocks ( Wang et al., 2018 ) , and DeeBERT and FastBERT allow easier language inputs to exit Transformer stacks early ( Xin et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2020 ) . These methods generally modify or train the model specifically for adaptive inference. We instead study frozen pretrained TSFMs without fine-tuning, directly bypass architecture-native blocks, measure realized GPU acceleration, and use a retrospective equal-budget oracle to test whether the identity of useful blocks varies across forecasting windows.

sections.heading: Models and executable units.
sections.text: We use pretrained amazon/chronos-bolt-base and google/timesfm-2.5-200m-transformers . Chronos-Bolt is T5-style; its first encoder block remains mandatory and blocks 1–11 are candidates. TimesFM is decoder-only with 20 candidate Transformer blocks. A disabled candidate returns its input before attention and feed-forward computation. Counters verify that inactive blocks are not called. With all candidates active, controlled and untouched forecasts agree exactly. We do not remove weights, so all parameters remain resident.

sections.heading: Data and metrics.
sections.text: We use ETTh1, Traffic, Weather, and Exchange ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2021 ) . Each example contains 512 context and 64 target steps. Selection uses disjoint calibration windows: 56 for ETTh1 and 64 for each other dataset. Evaluation uses 112, 512, 336, and 128 windows, respectively (1,088 total). We report normalized pinball loss over quantiles 0.1–0.9, with sMAPE and MASE as secondary metrics.

sections.heading: Selection and controls.
sections.text: Marginal importance is the calibration-loss change after removing one block. Backward greedy selection repeatedly removes the active block giving the lowest remaining calibration loss. No evaluation window affects selection. Chronos uses 11, 9, 7, 4, and 2 active candidates; TimesFM uses 20, 16, 12, and 8. We evaluate 20 deterministic random masks at each sparse budget. Balanced-global masks minimize the equal-weight mean calibration loss across datasets. Dataset-specific masks are used only at the main oracle budgets: 7/11 for Chronos and 12/20 for TimesFM.

sections.heading: Oracle and routing diagnostics.
sections.text: For each evaluation window, the oracle chooses the lowest-loss mask among four dataset-specific greedy masks and the balanced-global mask, all at equal cardinality. It is a retrospective upper bound, not an executable method. Confidence intervals use 2,000 bootstrap resamples of series/channel clusters. On Chronos only, small diagnostic classifiers use handcrafted temporal features or frozen context-only representations. Cross-validation groups windows from the same trajectory; leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) evaluation tests transfer to an unseen domain.

sections.heading: Systems measurement.
sections.text: We benchmark one NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB using five warm-ups and 30 repetitions with CUDA synchronization. We report median batch-1 latency and batch-32 throughput. For Chronos, quality uses greedy masks whereas systems measurements use cardinality-matched marginal masks; because candidate blocks have identical shapes, Chronos timing measures active-block-count cost rather than mask-specific latency. TimesFM condition order is randomized. Resident parameter bytes and peak CUDA allocation are recorded separately. Figure 1 summarizes the shared protocol and the architecture-specific executable units. Calibration windows validation periods Evaluation windows held-out test periods Marginal or greedy mask selection Chronos-Bolt tokenization Mandatory block 0 + selectable blocks 1–11 Frozen decoder quantile forecast TimesFM 2.5 RevIN + 32-step patches Selectable decoder blocks 0–19 Frozen output head quantile forecast Held-out quality execution counters A100 latency/throughput fixed mask fixed mask Figure 1: Methodology for both frozen TSFMs. Calibration data select static masks without test leakage; held-out windows then traverse genuinely bypassed architecture-native blocks. The same forecasts support quality, execution, latency, throughput, and retrospective equal-budget oracle analyses. Dashed arrows denote held-out inputs.

sections.heading: 5 Mask preference varies across windows
sections.text: Dataset-specific masks do not define stable specializations. TimesFM’s five 12/20 masks have pairwise Jaccard similarity 0.60–0.85, yet a dataset’s own mask is not reliably best: the Traffic mask is best on Exchange, the ETTh1 mask is best on Weather, and the Weather mask worsens Weather by 70.6%. Chronos shows the same qualitative instability. Dataset identity is therefore an inadequate routing rule. Figure 3 makes this instability visible after normalizing every cell to its dataset’s dense loss. A dataset-specialized pattern would place the best value on the native diagonal. Instead, off-diagonal masks frequently match or beat the native mask, and degradation is asymmetric. This does not imply one universal sparse network; it shows that dataset labels alone do not identify a consistently preferred one. Figure 3: Cross-dataset transfer at the main budget (7/11 Chronos, 12/20 TimesFM). Each cell is pinball-loss change relative to dense on the evaluation dataset; lower is better. Columns denote mask-selection origin. Despite weak specialization, the per-window oracle improves significantly over the best static equal-budget mask on every dataset and both models (Table 3 ). Relative gains range from 7.5–21.7% for Chronos and 3.2–17.1% for TimesFM; all cluster-bootstrap intervals exclude zero. All five masks win on every TimesFM dataset. Effective winning-mask counts are 4.68 on ETTh1, 4.68 on Weather, and 4.95 on Exchange. Traffic is less dynamic: its native mask wins 79.1% of windows and oracle gain is 3.2%. Input dependence is cross-model but heterogeneous. Figure 4 separates oracle magnitude from diversity. A positive gain with one effective winner would favor static selection; instead, most dataset-model pairs combine positive gain with several winners. TimesFM Traffic is the clearest exception. For Chronos, tied wins are divided evenly among tied masks before entropy is converted to an effective count, avoiding treatment of a tie set as a new mask. Figure 4: Oracle opportunity and diversity. Left: relative gain over the best static equal-budget mask with 95% series-cluster bootstrap intervals. Right: exponential entropy of the winning-mask distribution (maximum five); one denotes a single winner. Table 3: Oracle gain over the evaluation-best static equal-budget mask. All absolute-gain 95% series-cluster bootstrap intervals exclude zero. Model Dataset Static Oracle Relative gain Chronos-Bolt ETTh1 .2076 .1921 7.5% Traffic .1596 .1460 8.5% Weather .2056 .1717 16.5% Exchange .0158 .0123 21.7% TimesFM 2.5 ETTh1 .2178 .1915 12.1% Traffic .1763 .1706 3.2% Weather .1745 .1502 13.9% Exchange .0152 .0126 17.1% Chronos diagnostics test whether the oracle can be approached cheaply. Handcrafted features are harmful for mask selection. Frozen representations contain more within-domain signal: block-5 mean-plus-standard-deviation features reach 45.1% balanced mask accuracy and recover 29.5% of static-to-oracle gain, with a cluster bootstrap interval of 8.2–46.3%. However, LODO transfer mostly approaches chance and usually worsens selector loss. Later representations also consume part of the computation one hopes to save. The oracle demonstrates opportunity, not a practical router.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion and limitations
sections.text: Executable redundancy, real acceleration, and per-window preference occur in both a T5-style Chronos model and decoder-only TimesFM. Their magnitudes differ: TimesFM quality degrades sharply below 80% active on Traffic and Weather, while Chronos tolerates 7/11 better on average. Static sparsity must be calibrated per architecture and domain. Our scope is limited to two models, four univariate benchmarks, and one GPU type. Greedy masks are selected candidates, not optimal subnetworks. The oracle uses held-out losses retrospectively, and failed LODO diagnostics show that opportunity does not imply routability. Block skipping leaves weights resident, so we establish latency and throughput savings, not model-memory or energy savings. We do not report an edge-device benchmark. A dynamic system would require a cheap, transferable signal and end-to-end measurement including routing overhead; our experiments do not satisfy that requirement.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: Two architecturally different TSFMs perform removable block computation, and different equal-budget subnetworks are useful for different windows. Moderate static skipping reduces A100 latency by 11–13% with little aggregate quality change, despite substantial dataset-level variation. A retrospective oracle improves over the best static mask in both models, but dataset-specific transfer and unseen-domain routing remain unreliable. We find structured redundancy and input-dependent opportunity, not a deployable conditional-computation system.

Loss is normalized within model and dataset before averaging; latency is synchronized A100 batch-1 inference. 5 Mask preference varies across windows Dataset-specific masks do not define stable specializations. TimesFM’s five 12/20 masks have pairwise Jaccard similarity 0.60–0.85, yet a dataset’s own mask is not reliably best: the Traffic mask is best on Exchange, the ETTh1 mask is best on Weather, and the Weather mask worsens Weather by 70.6%. Chronos shows the same qualitative instability. Dataset identity is therefore an inadequate routing rule. Figure 3 makes this instability visible after normalizing every cell to its dataset’s dense loss. A dataset-specialized pattern would place the best value on the native diagonal. Instead, off-diagonal masks frequently match or beat the native mask, and degradation is asymmetric. This does not imply one universal sparse network; it shows that dataset labels alone do not identify a consistently preferred one. Columns denote mask-selection origin. Despite weak specialization, the per-window oracle improves significantly over the best static equal-budget mask on every dataset and both models (Table 3 ). Relative gains range from 7.5–21.7% for Chronos and 3.2–17.1% for TimesFM; all cluster-bootstrap intervals exclude zero. All five masks win on every TimesFM dataset. Effective winning-mask counts are 4.68 on ETTh1, 4.68 on Weather, and 4.95 on Exchange. Traffic is less dynamic: its native mask wins 79.1% of windows and oracle gain is 3.2%. Input dependence is cross-model but heterogeneous. Figure 4 separates oracle magnitude from diversity. A positive gain with one effective winner would favor static selection; instead, most dataset-model pairs combine positive gain with several winners. TimesFM Traffic is the clearest exception. For Chronos, tied wins are divided evenly among tied masks before entropy is converted to an effective count, avoiding treatment of a tie set as a new mask. Handcrafted features are harmful for mask selection. Frozen representations contain more within-domain signal: block-5 mean-plus-standard-deviation features reach 45.1% balanced mask accuracy and recover 29.5% of static-to-oracle gain, with a cluster bootstrap interval of 8.2–46.3%. However, LODO transfer mostly approaches chance and usually worsens selector loss. Later representations also consume part of the computation one hopes to save. The oracle demonstrates opportunity, not a practical router. 6 Discussion and limitations Executable redundancy, real acceleration, and per-window preference occur in both a T5-style Chronos model and decoder-only TimesFM. Their magnitudes differ: TimesFM quality degrades sharply below 80% active on Traffic and Weather, while Chronos tolerates 7/11 better on average. Static sparsity must be calibrated per architecture and domain. Our scope is limited to two models, four univariate benchmarks, and one GPU type. Greedy masks are selected candidates, not optimal subnetworks. The oracle uses held-out losses retrospectively, and failed LODO diagnostics show that opportunity does not imply routability. Block skipping leaves weights resident, so we establish latency and throughput savings, not model-memory or energy savings. We do not report an edge-device benchmark. A dynamic system would require a cheap, transferable signal and end-to-end measurement including routing overhead; our experiments do not satisfy that requirement. 7 Conclusion Two architecturally different TSFMs perform removable block computation, and different equal-budget subnetworks are useful for different windows. Moderate static skipping reduces A100 latency by 11–13% with little aggregate quality change, despite substantial dataset-level variation. A retrospective oracle improves over the best static mask in both models, but dataset-specific transfer and unseen-domain routing remain unreliable. We find structured redundancy and input-dependent opportunity, not a deployable conditional-computation system. References Ansari et al. (2024) A. F. Ansari, L. Stella, C. Turkmen, X. Zhang, P.
